description: This policy brief examines how Gulf bypass infrastructure is changing the strategic value of the Strait of Hormuz. It argues that the transition is from chokepoint indispensability toward differentiated bypassability, not from strategic importance to irrelevance. Crude oil can acquire substantial non-Hormuz capacity faster than petroleum products, while LNG remains structurally harder to substitute. The brief assesses Saudi westward pipeline options, UAE east-coast crude and port expansion, Hafeet Rail and Oman’s Gulf of Oman gateway role, crisis-era commercial rerouting, and the limits of claims that 50–70 percent of total energy flows could bypass Hormuz within two years. It concludes that bypass investment redistributes chokepoint risk across a wider network of pipelines, ports, railways, roads, terminals, and secondary maritime chokepoints.
abstract: The 2026 disruption of the Strait of Hormuz has accelerated Gulf efforts to reduce dependence on a single maritime gateway. Hormuz remains system-critical because of the scale of flows involved: in the first half of 2025, about 20.9 mb/d of oil and 11.4 Bcf/d of LNG transited the Strait. Saudi Arabia and the UAE currently provide the main crude-oil bypass capacity, with early-2026 estimates placing available capacity at about 4.7 mb/d, roughly 32 percent of the 2025 crude-and-condensate baseline. The UAE’s second Fujairah pipeline could raise this to about 6.2 mb/d by 2027, while Saudi Arabia is considering a further 1 to 2 mb/d expansion. These projects increase crude-oil bypassability, but their timing, effective throughput, and commodity mix remain uncertain. Adaptation is also extending beyond pipelines through Fujairah and other east-coast ports, the UAE–Oman Hafeet Rail project, and expanding road, rail, and multimodal routes around the Strait. The key constraint is that bypassability differs sharply by commodity: crude oil can be rerouted more readily than petroleum products, while LNG remains structurally harder to substitute. The brief concludes that Hormuz is becoming less singularly decisive, not strategically irrelevant, as the regional system shifts toward a more distributed network of pipelines, ports, railways, roads, and alternative maritime gateways.

methodology.framework_name: Differentiated Bypassability and Chokepoint Redistribution Framework
methodology.source_basis: Open-source policy analysis combining public infrastructure announcements, energy-flow estimates, international agency reporting, market and logistics reporting, and author calculations.
methodology.case_context: Strait of Hormuz disruption and Gulf bypass infrastructure development as of August 11, 2026, 00:27 ET, under the EPINOVA August 10 analytical-day convention.
methodology.core_problem: Whether new Gulf bypass infrastructure is reducing the strategic value of Hormuz by replacing it, or instead redistributing chokepoint risk across a wider network of pipelines, ports, railways, roads, terminals, and secondary maritime chokepoints.
central_claims: The transition is from chokepoint indispensability to differentiated bypassability, not strategic irrelevance.
Hormuz remains system-critical, but route exclusivity is eroding.
Bypassability differs sharply by commodity: crude oil > petroleum products > LNG.
Confirmed projects do not support a 50–70 percent shift in total energy flows within two years.
Bypass investment redistributes chokepoint risk rather than eliminating it.

dimensions.name: Traffic Centrality
dimensions.description: Scale of oil, LNG, and commercial flows through Hormuz
dimensions.observed_pattern: First-half 2025 flows included about 20.9 mb/d of oil and 11.4 Bcf/d of LNG.

dimensions.name: Substitution Capacity
dimensions.description: Physical and commercial capacity to redirect flows away from Hormuz
dimensions.observed_pattern: Early-2026 Saudi and UAE available crude-bypass capacity was estimated at about 4.7 mb/d.

dimensions.name: Commodity Differentiation
dimensions.description: Different substitution limits for crude oil, petroleum products, LNG, and commercial flows
dimensions.observed_pattern: Crude oil is most bypassable; LNG is least substitutable.

dimensions.name: Effective Throughput
dimensions.description: Actual volumes moved through alternative nodes rather than nominal capacity
dimensions.observed_pattern: Fujairah crude exports rose during crisis rerouting, but Gulf oil exports remained below prewar levels.

dimensions.name: Chokepoint Redistribution
dimensions.description: Shift of strategic weight from Hormuz to other nodes
dimensions.observed_pattern: Fujairah, Yanbu, Sohar, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez/SUMED, rail terminals, and land bridges become more important.

key_findings: Hormuz remains system-critical, but route exclusivity is eroding.
The strategic transition is from chokepoint indispensability to differentiated bypassability.
Crude oil can acquire substantial non-Hormuz capacity faster than petroleum products, while LNG remains structurally harder to substitute.
Early-2026 Saudi and UAE available crude-bypass capacity was estimated at about 4.7 mb/d, roughly 32 percent of the 2025 crude-and-condensate baseline.
The UAE’s planned second Fujairah pipeline could raise identified crude-bypass capacity to about 6.2 mb/d by 2027.
A crude-bypass share approaching 50 percent is plausible only under an upper-bound scenario in which the full proposed Saudi expansion is available for crude.
A 50–70 percent shift in total energy flows remains unsupported by confirmed infrastructure and analytically difficult to assess without a common energy basis.
Commercial logistics are already rerouting under crisis conditions.
Bypass investment redistributes chokepoint risk toward other nodes rather than eliminating it.
policy_recommendations: Separate crude oil, petroleum products, and LNG in resilience planning.
Measure resilience through effective throughput rather than nameplate capacity.
Assess bypass capacity as a network across Fujairah, Yanbu, Sohar, Bab el-Mandeb, Suez/SUMED, rail terminals, border crossings, and inland corridors.
Account for correlated disruption across pipelines, terminals, rail connections, and downstream maritime routes.
Distinguish strategic ambition from demonstrated capacity when evaluating 50–70 percent bypass claims.
Expect some diversification to persist after crisis conditions ease.
watchpoints: Realized incremental volumes through Yanbu and Fujairah compared with nameplate capacity.
UAE second Fujairah pipeline commissioning, terminal integration, and actual throughput after startup.
Saudi expansion FID, contract awards, interconnection plans, and capacity-access arrangements.
UAE LNG diversification project configuration, FID, EPC award, feed-gas plan, site selection, and construction schedule.
Hafeet Rail completion and recurring freight use through Sohar.
Persistence of crisis-era land bridges, port calls, contracts, and customs routines after shipping conditions improve.
Correlated risk across Bab el-Mandeb, Suez/SUMED, Fujairah, Yanbu, Sohar, and inland logistics infrastructure.
